Eight miles of the iron road are set apart on the Camden and Am- boy Railway, New Jersey, for the purpose of making an experiment. Two locommiven are in coarse of conetruction, which, with stationary engines at the terminal onion., are expected belie in working order early in the month of Sep- tember. If the trials to be made yield satisfactory results, it is in contemplation to apply the electric BVWPIII to the Elevated Railway, which, running through the etre. of New York, causes, in its present state, a vast ded of annoy- once and great inconvenience by reason of emoky locomo- tives, gaseous exhalation., and an imolerable rumbling noise. The electric engines are calculated to minimise these complaint., they will prove less noisy, emit no smoke or atenni, nor fill the air with cinder+. In addition thereto they will introduce great economy in the working expenses of railways. The electricity which supplies the nmtive power is generated at stationary engines, and thence trann- initted to the electric maor, placed on the line, which in turn gives motion to the wheels, a copper wire of the thick- nese of three-quarter of an inch answering every purp.e. The motor is very nearly the Paine as the one in use for the electric light, and the power ea mysteriously created is corn. municated to the wheels by means of leather bands. The motive power may be detached at will, a powerful brake works In connection with it, and the train comes to a standatill without any apparent effort It has been esti- mated that the city of NOW York would require no more than ei- electric stations for the use of the four railways which comprise the system of the city traffic. There 10 no immediate necessity to place the electric stations in close proximity to the railway track. The benefit arising there- from in important, inasmuch as it admits the selection of a locality where facilities cm be secured for an economical supply of water. Each of the six mations will he required to furnish its quota of power, each quota to be graduated acconling to the re ,liiretnente of the traffic. The stationary engines are to In worked on au extremely ecooomical plan. Engineers and firemen. as now employed on loco- motives, may be dixpensed with. THE EDUCATION OP ANCIENT JEWISH CHILDREN. In • paper read at the recent Sunday school centenary, at Earleetown, Mr. P. M. Cempbell on the education and in- strection of children among the ancient Jews according to the Bible and Talmud, says that the most interediag period of Jewish history is certainly that which preceded the advent of Christianity. Jewish society then offered the most extraordinary moral and intellerotual state that the human race has ever pawed through. Pressed on all sides by • powerful enemy, and one to whose power in spite of indomitable courage they could not hope to break, and promoting itaelf 'wherever they went and for the second time, and for ever being torn from that country so dear to them, and which had cod them sack paina to conquer, the Jewish people summoned all their force and all their energy in view of this new and terrible proof. However feeble and isolated they were, they would not perish nor their indiridnality end cmae to play a part among the nations. They were able by the strength of this force to resist mropMtioes and seduction, as well sat menaces and permeations and Hier lived intact and uncontaminated, and the laud, of the rimmed book the Talmud Torah, became thee the object of all their thought. and a most lively solicitude. Academie. were founded for the study of the book, and it formed the beau. of all education. In the first place it was necemary to in- clude, aa being /earners, the children of Israel during the biblical period, when for along time education was purely dorneatic then in the mcond placethe important pedagogue movement, which was developed among the Jews Irene the time of Ears to the final revision of the Talmud from 458 C. C. to 500 A. no. After reviewing the domestic life of the Hebrews the emayist proceeded to my that that which formed the basis of their education was moral and religion. teaching. Among all nations the direction given to education depends upon the 'dean formed by them of when contaitutes• perfect man. With the Ronsons it is • valiant soldier, inured to fatigue, sad obedient to discipline, with the Athenisn. it is • man who unims in himself that beautiful harmony of the perfection of moral and physical worth. Among the Hebrews the perfect man Cr the pious and virtuous [114.11, capable of attaining to the ideal of the Hebrew people, described by God himself. The firm duty prescribed by the Mosaic Law is the reepect doe to father and mother. The Divine Voice uttered this ammeod from the eummit of Mount Sinai, " Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy day. may be long upon the lead which the Lord thy God giveth then." They afterwards isspired the children with the love of labour, the shame of idlenette, the repugnance for unwhole- some pleimures, kindness faille poor and didremed, and above all the fear of God, which is the beginning of all wisdom. The first aim of Hebrew education was to make men fear God and keep his commandments, the second being to make them good citizens, no part of education being better regu• lated in the nation. They were earnestly recommended to teach their children their faith In the great deetiny and mission of Israel, and to mete them learn it by heart by writing and repeating the last eongof Moose in Deuteronomy, 32nd c4ipter, which celebrator in poetical accenm the exalted levet.' God for bin people, and in which God avows for the descendants of the patriarchs the same love and promises hi. etmnal protection. While all these interpretations rest on a foundation more or lesa just, we are enly able to coachede with all the more corminty that they were centres of instruction. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY AUGUST 28.1 MR

Tan discontented Irish members are bent upon making the utmost capital out of the .tion of the Home of Lords in throwing out the Irish Compensa- tion Disturbance Bill. Upon this peg they hang a new grievance, and are in it an excuse for delivering wild harangues to excitable crowds, and for badger lag the Government that h. striven 80 zealously to give to Ireland not only the Irish Compensation Disturbance Bill, but evinced a readiness to accord to Ireland every measure of relief that justice and reason dictate. Mr. Diflon has this week bearded in the HOOPS of Coninions the Chief Secretary for Ireland upon the common's offered by the latter upon the Kildare speech of the former, but Mr. Forster reiter- ated his amertion that the speech was not only wicked, but cowardly in the settie that by hints and innendoes he advised • suffering and distressed people to resort to illegal practices which he would not him- self venture to do. Finding himself secure from proeecution, Mr. Dillon declared that be would repeat his Kildare addreas throughout Ireland. Such addresses as that are calculated to inflame the paa SiOne of the people groaning under the burden of distress and oppression, and to incite them to lewlmsnens ; and to put down any insurrectionary movement the Government are determined to spare no coot or pains. Punishment, grief, and late will therefore fall upon thooe who give one to such wild language as that of the member for Tipperary. Would-be martyrs have existed all ages, and it may be that thate who venture to ooneider tbemaeves the embodiments of the opinion of respectable and reflecting Irish people, and as the haaventhorn apostles of Irish liberty, think they are pursuing a righteous course in delivering heated speeches to excited crowds and in harsesing any and every Government which, however friendly it may be towards them, does not see eye to eye with them. Men el tbis stamp are not the true friends of Ire- land ; they are most dangerous to her weal and ta&pneas. By their persietent ravings and diaeon- mateelnette they outrage and • trp the generous! impulses of those who would stead by them in the ' hour of need and peril, and who would struggle to Ware them justice. If Mr. Dillon fan.es he is likely to win the admiration and sympathy of sensible law- abiding citizens when he recommends the wretched : peasants he is addressing to inflict horrible tortures npon innocent cattle which chance to be the property ' of the owncre of Irish soil, or when he gives vague ' hint. to aggrieved tenants to attack the lives of lauds lords, he is mietaken. He may profess indifference to I: English mit tenons, but all dispetstionat et Irishmen must be disgusted with the advocacy of hamstringing of I innocent cattle and with suggest ions to have reeourt ft to practices which the common conscience of humanity abhorr. It may be valorous to din into the ears of the Government that rest year the questioe.of the legality ' of bearing armsin Ireland would be toiled by rifle cluba tesching people how to shoot, and that it would be ; seen where the cowardith lay; but it would be I foolhardiness en the part of those who. cause Mt Dillon asemnee to be the champion of to adopt hie advice, as they would find to their that If Irish members were wise in their day and gene- ration they would aid instead of perpetually! badgering and hindering the Government which has ' shown a disposition to extend all possible relief to Ire- land. At every turn the would- be martyrs in Ireland's I mime raise the flag of obstruction to useful legislation, end the Tories, from whom they have reoeired no• thing but snubs, coercive laws, and powder and shot, are onlyffoo ready to kin them in hampering the Govern- ment in their efforts to forward the programme of civil and religious liberty. It is not enough for fire-eaters of the Dillon and Parnell type tote told by a reepon• sible member of the Cabinet that the Government recognised that the relations between landicrd and tenant in Ireland absslutely required improvement; that the Government had endeavoured to secure that improvement; that the Government had not in the , slightest degree changed their opinion as to the ttaz I fortunate calamity that they thought Ind overtake. the Irish Compensation Disturbance Bill, which they I had panted through the House of Commons, but which ; was rejected by the Lords, and that if need be the Government would request special powers to deal with acts of injustith which the Compensation Disturbance Bill would have wet All these declarations and all the practical evidences of willing.us to afford relief to Ireland by the Government amounted to nothing with the would- be martyrs, who aro perpetually "orating be- muse, like spoiled children, they cannot have . everything they cry for. They have consumed this week one•balf of the time, at least, the Ho.e of Commons ought to have devoted to tuneful ; legislation in obstruction and in tlamouring for a .parate Government for Ireitted, when they know well that in the proemnt disposition of the Logi, /ature it is hopeless to expert any Such COn• cession. Thursday night's proceedings furnish an example of the persieteney tif the Irish membersto obstruct business by a factions opposition to the! estimatee for the support of the Irish con etabulary. At nine o'clock ymterchm (Friday). thing the House, which had been sitting/Imm four o'clock on the pre- vious afternoon, was still in committee of atipply. As Mr. Forster remarked the other evening law, how- ever unsatisfactory it maybe, will have to be observed in Ireland as elsewhere as it f' iStfi ; and if the Powers of the Government are not sufficient to enforce ob. esmance of that law, special powers will have to , be given to the Executive. Anarchy cannot be per• mitted to run riot in the Sister Isle any more than in England, Scotland, or Wake, and these who entourage it are enemies and not friends of the people whom they profms to be leaders of. If, instead of seeking popularity or notoriety by being noisy both in and out of Parliament, and innbetructing legialation at every possible opportunity, the profeseed friends of! Ireland would calmly and consistently aid the most friendly Government Ireland has ever had they would gain more for the happiness and prosperity of Ireland than they are likely to do by the course they are now pursuing, for by it they attreage instead of winning the sympathy of those who would gladly help in the removed of the too many grierancea under which Ireland undoubtedly suffer..

The annual election connected with the Runcorn Board of Commls.ioners takes place on the 2nd instant. The to tiring nembers are Messrs. F. McDougall, William Lyon, Matthew Steele, Philip Speakman, and Robert Shaw, all of whom, I believe, seek re-election. These gentlemen are well known to the ratepayera, who, I on lerstood from Dr. MeHonaall's remarks, were to be called together in their thousands to protest, in bore of thunder, against the un- warrantable action of a large majority of the member., °p- i posed to 1 wonderful tninority of three, in making en inexpensive arrangement with the Liverpool Corporation, by which in time to coin° the town may be guaranteed a supply of vedter, in case they rrtmiro it. All successful men net dietlaguished by foresight, and the business men who! fires from hand to mouth and does not calculate on future is generally what the Americans call • one- horsedeam man, and reidain trcAdAeB any one. The meeting of ra,,A,e,A he. oat beast called and I ...opus. it may be taken In; granted that this course bee been adiTteli from prudential resorts. I think that all who have watched the course pureued he Mr. Robert Shaw Sill,o he has occupied a vat at the Boaril. must Admit that hie strong common sense and business ability have been conspicuously ahown tmon many occasions, and it wilt be a matter of regret to the town if him services 'Mould be lord to the town. A rumour has been circulated that • certain email ',Action of the rate- payers would try to injure Mr. Philp Speakman's chances of emcees, because of the prominent part he has taken upon a:certain public question. I. however, think there is no doubt that the great majority of the ratepayers are thoroughly satisfied with Mr. Speakman's course of conduct ; and they recognise that Ins labours have had no email Snare in reducing the third class farce between Runcorn and Liverpool ; in c.tuelog the decinion to put a wide footpath seines Waterloo bridge, and materially improve tbi.etrnctnrn. the condition of which has fort long period , been so disgraceful in winterly weather and, above all, in • carrying to to succeasful an issue the negotiatione with the Liverpool Corporation upon the water question. Mr. Speak. mun,inteernrentteeenntiallV nod.Pre.eminently those oft Runcorn gentleman ; and I ventore to predict that he will stand well on the day of election. At the public meeting held in St. Paul's Wesleyan Runcorn, on the evening of the celebration of the centenary of Sunday school., Mr. William Handley elicited from the , chairman, Mr, John Simpson, Hi, he wee a Runcorn lad. . This onnouncement appears to have caused a little surpriee !amongst many of the audience and townspeople, many of the oldest of whom appeared to labour under the idea that . Mr. Simpson was an alien as far 00 Runcorn woe concerned. , An old inhabitant informs the writer that Mr. Simpson wan born in Church-street, iinmediately opposite the Eraminer office, hut at the age of three or four years he left the town with hie father, and removed either to Lancashire or York- shire. He believed it vu. the latter county, but on this point my information isnot definite. Sir. Simpson has been a moot euccessful man of business, and though in one im. portant speculation his usually ehrewd judgment appeared to fail him, he is considered one of the wealthiest new in the district. lie is also a great lover of books, and hie library' at Frodsham, where his reeidence is the envy of many a bi bl iographer. It would be a glorious thing for Runcorn if Mr. Simpson, with his vast wealth, could be influenced to follow the ex- ample of Mr. Taylor, of Wigan. and provide the town with a Free Library building, and no make his name to be a sweet savour in the memory of future generations of Runcomians.

A discussion of considerable importance took place at the last meeting of the Runcorn Burial Boani, which resulted In the important decision being arrived at that in future the cemetery should be opened for Sunday funerals. I think I may flatter myself that the observations which hare from time to time appeared under "Flacons" upon this subject have had the effect of throwing • little light on what is really required from Christians in the matter or Sabbath ebeervence, and it would probably seem somewhat moguler to some of your readers if I did not refer to the meeting. To Mr. Coleburn is due the credit of bringing the desirability of opening 'he cenwery nn Sundaos forward, and consider. able praise is also due to him for the conciliatory manner in which he appears to have argued the question, which in the hands of a gentleman with less tact would hare no doubt raised for more bitternees of feeling than what appear. to have characterised the discussion. On looking at the report of the proceedings tom amnewhat .toniehed to find that Mr. Norman is conepicuous by his absence from the meeting, and I am the more surprined at this, as I underetond he was likely to take a prominent part. Mr. Geo. Marshall seert:s to hare posed as • martyr to his particular opinions, and to have been under some Impression that if Sunday funerals were allowed the floodgates of immorality would be oponol and the day ba grossly profaned. I regret to find thee Mr. Marshall, who, I believe, is some. what of • It idical in politics, should have ranged himself so distinctly on the side of the sticklers for the letter of the law, who often Infertile spirit of a command. The scriptares say that "the letter killeth." The speech de- livered by him is mark, ,t by too strong a tone, a kind of as- sumption that he is confident he is right, and, of course, that every other member of the Burial Board in wrong. He even goes further than this, and throws out hints—mf a very broad nature too—that he is very much astonished that gentlemen professing to be Christians should dare to take such a course ; and no good as nava that if the privilege be grantee% Runcorn, spiritually, will be given over to the Prince of Harkness, and the continental Sunday will be immedi- ately established. The Scribes and Pharisees were the great observers of times and the givers of tithes in their days. The Pharisee@ received& terrible shack to their feelings when they new Christ attempting to do good on the Sabbath and they:in their presumptions self.righteousness, at once set Him down no one who was not a servant of God. Os another occasion these wiseacres solemnly objected to Christ's die- ciples °lucking the ears of corn on the Sabbath ! What a frightful deweration of the holy far ! They were told that the Sabbath wea made for man, and not man for the Sab- bath. Certainly some Procisioninta would, at first sight, have been led to think that the Pharisees were right in their ideas of Sabbath observance, and that their strict attention to every tittle of ritual or set otwervance would have been edmi4cd by the Saviour, but Its said thefwere simply blind guides. who paid tithe of mint and anise and cumtnin, but omitted the weightier matters of the are, judgment, mercy. and faith: and described them aa serpents, ... generation of vipers, and asked them how they should wept the darnaation of hell. Then Mr. Marshall went on to say that If the Board took ouch C step it would only prove the truth of the statement of one whew.. an authority, that the town woo one of the most godless in England. I should very much like to Imow who this great authority'' was, for in my opinion his k 110•110,14. Of fh, tomes of the United kingdom must be of e most contracted description. It sounds very much like the remark of some excited en. %busiest who has a far greater share of emotion than common

tones; and it may be emphatically condemned xs • most grow libel on the some and its inhabitants. Think of Seven Dials, London of DeAnsgate, Manchester ; of Scotland-road, Liverpool, and compare these with the peacefulness of a Runcorn Sabbath. Then the speaker quoted the fourth commandment, and dealt with it as if we were tiviog under the Jesvieh economy, instead of node, a New Covenant in which one of the writers—St. Paul—suns let no man judge you in respect to meats, Sabbath days, or holy days, which but a shadow of things to come. Our theological ! friend next gave his hearers a Scriptural exposition, which • I give in full for fear your readereshould not have the benefit of it. He meld :—"lt was the duty of Christiana to follow the Saviour. who, when speaking to one of hie disciple, and telling him to follow llim, received the reply, 'Let me fret go and bring my dead.' To this Christ at once odd,. Let Ohs dead bury their dead. Follow thou me.' On this prin.' I ciple, he maintained that when work meld be done on other days than the Sabbath, it ought to be." What no in. ference for one who is a local brother ! Let me throw a little light on the benightel mental condition of Mr. Marshall's conception of the meaning of this passage : and, as he Is • Wesleyan methodist, I will do so by quoting Dr. Adam Clarke's commentary upon it. The learned doctor, who was probably one of the profoundest scholars w/to ever livol, says in regard to the person by whom the worths were spoken (" Another of His disciples ") . This does not nsean any of the twelve, but one of those who were constant hearers of our Lord's preaching the name of disciple being common to all theee who professed to believe in Him. ' gory my father : ' probably his father sem old, and appa- rently near death ; Jut it was a maxim among the Jews, that, if a man hat any duty to perform to the dead, he wae, for that tiine, free from the observance of any other precept or duty. . • Let the dead bury their dead.' It was mind for the Jews to consider a man as dead who had de- parted from the precepts of the Law and, on this ground, every tranegreasor was reputed a dead man. Our Lord's saying, being in common use, had nothing difficult in it tot Jew. Natural death Is the eeparation of the body and soul ; spiritual death, the separation of God and the soul; men who live in nisi are dead to liod. Leave the spiritually dead to bury their natural dead. All the common officee of life m ly be performed by any pereon ; to preach the glad tidings nf the Kingdom of God is grunted hut to a few, and to these only In an especial call ; these should immediately abandon worldly concerns and employments, end give themselves wholly up to the work of the minietry." Here in. passage which, according to the commentator, proves that the Jews held a nun who had any duty to perform to the dead as free from the observance of any other precept or duty ; and Mr. Marshall actually quotes it to establish hie own position. All I can say is, that, in my humble opinion, if the expositions of the obligatoriness of Sabbath oheer' o,,flceunrcieen by this gentleman are no more valuable than his exposition of this particular passage, it is quite clear that his theoloxic attainments are not of a very valuable description, and that the special evmination which the Wesleyan Conference Repotted to institute in the case of all local preachers might possibly provedf use in his particular cue. lam afraid of trespassing upon your space, or !might go no to notice the attack of Mr. Marshall upon the member. of the Friendly Societies, which were so well defended by Mr. Littler, Why Mr. Marshall should have gone out of hie way to irritate a number of nano who are no influential in tbe town, I cannot understand. lneottolusiuo, I may say that this gentlernaa talks About his own conscience lie if no .ther member on the Board had one, and I ebould adviee him to try to ayoild this apftimen of bad taste in the future. There appeared in • loon contemporary of Wednes- they last, under the above heading, • etort article which for toadyiam, iipsoranee, and misrepresentation, I never saw exceibil. In thin precione effusion there occur, the follow- ieg. in reference to Mr. Bright, the chancellor of the Duchy, bovind refuwal to confirm the nomination of Aldermin Pickmere *se borough magistrate. The f ollow ing is what your contemporiry arye,--" It appear* that Mr. Bright'eattaition has tre,.n called by memorial to the fact that Major Pick- hold, en ordinary Beence as well as that of a wholemle wino and spirit merchant having purcheeed, hut not used the license of a place near, but which has been closed; and further, that owing to Mr. Bright'e antipathy to licenaed victualler. the 'Mayor will not be able to qualify as • per- manent magistrate." Now in reply M the that statement, it ia well known that Mr. Pickmere holds an ordinary public- house Beet. for his chop in Bridge-street (where he resided until very lately), where people have • right to go and call for what they want, and drink it on the premises, and that lionise in granted to hire annually by the InaMetrates, and I was pre- sent at the sennions room last Tuesday week, when I heard his name called out along with other. to whom a Nemce wae granted to cell ale, wine, and opirits by retail, to be drunk on or eff the premieee. Mr. Picktnereki ie eseentially a retail businem, and he in no more a wholesale wine and spirit merchant than • many other ordinary publicans in Warrington and elsewhere. What becotne., then, of thin bareehmed amertion that " Mr. Pickmere only holds an ordinary licence fora place that is elowd and not used?" I menot believe that the writer of that article can be so ignor- ant as not to know that no magistrates would grant. retail license to • premises "that was closed and not need." But if be is ignorant of it he ootlitt mu bnael,e,oa,lOl himself, ...I II be Is not igeorant of it he ought al to be ashamed of himself, for he in wilfully trying to mislead. Now for the other Agee-Goo. that °M-. Bright, owing to hie antipathy to licensed victuallers, 1.1 prevented Mr. Pickmere from mudifying as a permanent magistrate." Mr. Bright has acted front no each unworthy pereonal motives. Ile has only aeled on Gm very eatne rule laid down long ago, and obeened by hie predecessors in office of both political mations, via, not to sanction the election of any licensee victualler to the mayieterial bench ; and very properly no, too. Now, Mr. Pickmere has alwaye been a strong sup- porter of Sir Gilbert Grernall'a, who wait anaioue enough to have made tmi,o a borough magiatrate. This is no new thine; it ia well known, and for your neutral" contemporary to try to toddle Mr. Bright with the responsibty at hevialt tehmed to make Mr. Pickmere a borough magintrate, and to impale an un- worthy motive to him, via, " hie hated of licensed victuallers," is diet event, and a libel upon one of the noblest men in England. Mr. Picktnere is placed in a painful and humiliating poeition, and I am sorry for it, because Mr. Pickmere personally is quite as worthy of being placed on the borimgli bench as any of the three gentlemen who were nominated with him by the Town Council; but his over zealous and not over dimreet friends are alone responsible for it, although he himmlf cannot be entirely abeolved Iron, blame. BM% HAIM Fiternest..—The second annual rural testi. val, promoted by the members of the North Ashton Bram Band. was held on Saturday, in a field in the occupation of Mr. John Rigby, llownall Ureen. M.r.M•nrio TarLoa moved the following resolnlion, of which he had given notice :—That the members of the School Board having noticed a report in the local preen that the Widnes local Board intend to invite mwtile who malty vialt fairs with Worse, stall., nterty-go-rounds, Ao,top.teaoieit to Widow in the month el September next; that this Board prolesio against the poblic invitation by the hoed Board, ia such visit tends to damage the morels of th,freople of WkIPIPA, especially the children of the town, end het the clerk be instracted to send a copy of this protent to the Chairman of the Local Board." It. said that the subject had been discueeed in many way, during the net two or three years, inciuding the ventilation of it to the local preen. It had also coine prominently under the notice of the Local Boned. Ile believed that the only defence offered at the la, ineetingef the Local /Want for the action which it 1.3 e proposed to take, IVAn that the fair brought in the annual AUIII of 030. Well, be did not believe that if tha pceple who came to the fair from other places were marched ae they came into the town that w much money an that would be found upon them. The mull was that it was quite evident the money referred to came out of the pockets of the ratepayem, by whom he believed it would be (mind a saving to contribute this sum in some .thier way. Some couple of years ago he had • conversation with Mr. Brown, one if the tnembern of the Local Board, who told him that he intended to take eome Wows null the object of trying to prevent that body taking the fair under their protection in the future, and he had Dinoe done err, but his efforts had not been crowned with suc- cess. He (the Meeker) had nothing to say about any indi- vidual member upon the Local Boaral who might have taken • prominent part in the discussion of the question at their meetings. lie might, however, ear he believed that one gentleman had been somewhat prominent in the expression of his views in favour of inviting the fair people, though he Scarcely appeared to defend hie action born the point of view from which the members of the School Board seemed to look at the queetion. It sew certainly a very weak argument to saw that the fair ought to be continued because it brought in • Sum Of AP yearly. He personally thought it was the duty of the School Board,ae a public I,ody, to protest against the action of the members of their local Parliament, and in the interest of the children who were under their control. At all event, he could not agree with the course which appeared to have been adopted by the Local Board of inviting those people to visit the town. Rev. FA".lllolFinatiAN wconded the motion, and said be could, to a great extent, support elm( Mr. Taylor had wid. Ever since he bail been a member of the Board he had felt . Strongly on 'his matter, and even if he were not a member of it, he should still protest against such a saturnalia an the fair being invittal to make its tonic in Widnes yearly. He, however, thought that they could not go into the moral part of the question, although there might lea great deal said upon that. It was most unfortunate that the fair eliould take place in the town during the very month when the ex- aminations were held. Mr. DFACON agreed very much with Mr. Taylor and the Rev. Father Finegan had said, but he considered that the objeetion of the Board to the fair Ought to he placed upon a different basis. Mr. Taylor hind spoken upon the effect which the holding of the fair had riloon the ettentlance of children at school. Now he (Mr. Deacon) had not to hand the atten• dance at the voluntary whools of the town, but, looking at that at the Board Schmitt, he could not find that the atten- dance had been materially decreased during the time of the fair. In fact, the attendaace did not seem to be effected in any marked degree, and on this ground be thought that the oon-attendmce of the children should be made a basis of opposition to the holding of the fair. Notwithstanding what the Rev. Father Finegan had said, he conaidered they were thoroughly justified in speaking of the moral effects of the fair. An to drunkennew, he might say that, w far as he coold diacover. the fair neither increased one decreased it. He had asked the opinion of sevend people who visited the fair onto what they thought of it, and they spoke strongly against it, on the ground of its immorality and tendency to corrupt. He had pleasure in supporting the motion. At one time he was in favour of the fair. as be felt very strongly skit the workpeople of Widnes were placed at a great disadvantage as regarded amusemrnts, when compared with Boma towns It was not fair to expect all of them to be educated, and, therefore, capable of deriving pleaeure from intellectual sources: and, in the present elate of mat- tern, the workingmen of the town appeared to have nowhere logo, AA long as be thought the amusement balanced the effects of the fair, he was decidedly in favour of upholding it, but he hart come to the conclusion that the evil effects far outweighted ivy govt resulting from it. Of courw, even if the Local Board refused to give their countenance out, it would not proveM the people who frequented the fair from visiting the town, Ind it would not favour them congrega- ting in one spot, A. wee at present the caw, unless some landowner 'Mould decide to permit them to come upon his

land. Mr. HARTLAND thought the remarksof Mr. Taylor as to the effect which the fair had upon the ratepayers very plausible, for the money pail be the fair people really came out of the pockets of the townkpeople. In too many cases the very people who spent their money at such a time were those who omld not afford to to to, and when the rent col- lector went to their houses the following week he was told that the sum which should have lwen paid for rent had been spent. It often took ten or twelve weeks to make up the deficiency, and all thin tirne the poor children were suffering. They ought to keen all the money they could in Whinee at the present time, as the rat. were so very high. Mr. Mama Straw thought that Mr. Deacon's figures could hardly be considered complete, and that the subject was so broad befitt would require A very mach faller 0010. meet than they had had presented to them in order to show the effect ot the holding of the fair upon their schools. He believed that the fair affected the attendance very con- sidwahly after It took place, and that it also had an influence on the school fees. When they considered the wins thee were paying for the education of people whom they con- sidered were not able to educate their own children, and what the Hoard were doing to improve the morals of the people by education, he was of opinion they would come to the conilusion that it was their duty le protest against any- thing which they believed would interfere with the work they had in hand. He did not consider that providing a fair catne within the legitimate budneas td the Local hoard, and they could not do it under any Act of Parliament. The members were not sent to the Board-room to provide this Find of demoralinlng amusement for the lowest orders in Widnes—in fact the very people with whom the School Board found the weatest difficulty in dealing. They felt it their duty to protest againet the general invitation which the Local Hoard offered to the clam of people who frequented fairs to visit the town. In conclusion, he hoped that the Lotal Board would tee their way to take no active part, at WI events, in promoting the fair, and that if the people who usually frequented it did come in the ordinary way (over which the Hoard could have no control), they would employ what power they bed either to control or entirely prevent the excessive evils which flowed from such gatherings. The resolution sem carried unanimously, after which the proceedings terminated.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A PRISONER AT WARRINGTON BRIDEWEI,L A sudden death of • prisoner occurred at the Warrington I Bridewell on Tuesday morning Mead eight o'clock. It appears that at 6-15 p.m. on Saterday at the attention of P.C. Clynes was called to a woman named Mar,aret Marti- i son, 40 years of age, lying drunk in Wilson Patten.treet. Wan the awistance of P.C. Edwards she was brought to the police A 16013, where site w. charged and locked up. After getting up on Sunday morning abeam:leered robe, and collected,and remained so al: day. However, when placed in She dock at 10-30 ant., on Monday, it was observed that she rambied in her speech, sod seemed unable to mall.< her ',oration. The prusoner's Oilerdn-law, who was in court, offered to take her home, but afWrwards said she would not take her home, but to the elation, and would pay her fare to Southport, where she resided. To this course tfie chief con- stable Mr. Hunt) ohjected, as he thought the wee unfit to be it large, and the prisoner was ordered to be put down again until the following morning, the Bench believingthat 24 hours freedom from drink would bring her round. and that her friend, might take charge of her. At 8-45 pm. on Monday, when visited in the cells by P.C.'s Wheatley and liendy, the reserve nen, she appeared considerably better, but acted very etrangely in bee manner. ton Tuvaday morning it 7-30 she get up, and came into the woinen'e dav ward. washed hermit in warm water, and walked about the Yard until 9 o'clock, when she had warn. warm tea for breakfast, but could not eat anything, She eat down and drank about half of the tea, put the can on the thor. lay down and died immediately without a groan or struggle. At 7.30 p on Monday, tl.se deceased asked the chief constahle for a I whiskey, which he gave her : Ana at 8 o'clock on Tuesday morning Mrs. Hunt observing the deceasel ecemed to be very ill sent for the sergeant with a view of getting medical aid. The inquest, touching the death of the deceased. was held by Mr. C. E. Isrdfield. on 'flared., at the Marquis of tiranby public-house, Cburch-strect. The first Willlc•S wan . . . .

Mr. S. Hunt, chief constable, whose evidence confirmed the statement given absve. Mr. John Newcombe, banker's clerk, 33, Wilson Patten- . street, Warrington, said that, on Saturday evening, aboet half-past six, he saw the deceased in Wile. Patten-street, in the act of falling over on her side. A lad, who was pas- sing, helped her up, and put her against the railings, but in a few minutes she tottered and fell back upon her head. She was picked up again, and this was repeated. The witness then brought an officer, who took her into custody. Dr. Swrkey Smith stated that he male• posi-nrortvm ex- amination on Tuesday afternoon. He found across the fore- head a cwetusol euperficial wound. The upper portions of the arms had linger marks, as if the deceased had been tightly gripped, and on both shins were several dark bruises The cause of death was serous apoplexy under the mem- branes, and the ventricles at thetas, There was no eff tlaloll of blood, but there was great congestion. The bruises had nothing to do with the cause of death. The lungs not heart were fairly The stomach was empty. The liver wasertensively diseased in what was called The "nutmeg state." The other organs appearel fairly healthy. The nutmeg Mate indicated a long-contmued over-indulgence in 11pirit001101 liquors. The deceas,d had some of the symptoms of de/trio at tremens. People who were in the habit of in- dulging in exceseive drinking often die very suddenly. Had he been proscribing for her, he woutd, in all probability, hare given her just what the chief constable bone given her, as her Moinach would have rejected any solid food. A son of the deceased said that his mother left Southport on Saturday to go on a visit to some friend, at Lyinm. She was quite sober, and was not given to drink. This state- ment IVRA corroborated by another witness. The jury returned • verdict of death from apoplexy.

Mr. Driffield, the district county coroner, held an inquest at the Haydock Lodge Retreat on Thursday, on the body of Mrs. Jane Vernon, a widow lady who Lae been an inmate during the past six Months. In August, 1878, the husband of the deceased died, and the circumstance no affected her mind that some fern months afterwards she ettempted to put an end to her ezietance. Acting under medical advice, her relations placed her under Dr. Lister's control, end eincetbet time she haa lived Cl the lodge, under the personal superin- tendence of a nurse who never left her night or dAy. On the day of her admietion and on the following ntorning she attempted to kill herself, bet made no further effort to do Any harm until Monday morning I tete alien ehe overpowered her attendant end threw herself into A duck-pond some short distance away from the house, and before further araietance could be obtained life was found to he extinct. The follow- ing evidence was taken. Mr. Janne Show, pliyeinian and surgeon, reeident medical officer Cl the lodge, mid the deceased lady was a widow 55 years ef age. She had been a first-claw private patient from February this year. Witness prodnced the order upon which she was received. which showed that she ctme (nun ITushingham, in Cheseire, and was described ae • suicidal I , patient. Witnees knew title to he the ease, and deceased I . had &Deity. a apecial attendant with her, also wearing gloves i during the night. Twice preyiouely she had attempted tol ! kill hernelf, once on the Itlth of February, • fortnight sifter • her admission when she tried to strangle hereelf, and egain the morning after when she tried to jump over the oalu- : atrades of the stairs. Since then nhe had made no ist tempt re Scene herself. On Monday morning witness wee away on a holiday, and when he returned deceased was dead. Dr faster wee, however, at home, and wee early in attendance. Deceased's private attendant, Elisabeth donee, wan with her at the time of the occurrence, Ind one of the private patients named Wild was near, and took the body out of the water. Tnis patient was convalescent and able to give evidence The pit where the occurrence happened was in the grounds and wee called the duck pond. It wee protected altnost all round by a wire fence, a small portion being left open for , cattle.

—EI izalwtb donee said she waa an attendant at the lodge, where she hail been the post six months, corning about q week after the admission of the deceased. ‘Vitnese was in personal attendance on the deceased for three months, and again for about • month, the time between them two loccasiims Ellen Matheson being in charge. Shortly after her admiesion witneas found deceased on the table in her , bedroom trying to strangle herself. and the next morning she tried to get over the glair balustrades and on bath occasions she prevented her doing harm to herself. On Mon•' day morning, as mu her usual custom. deceased went out at eleven o'clock. attnarently in her customary state, witness having noticed nothing different in her manner. Witness and decmaed were walking near the pond, witneaa having hold of deceased'e left arm, when deceased dragged witnem over the wire fence and down the slope towards the pit, and threw herself into the water. Witness called for help, and Henry Hale, the kitchen gardener, jumped into the water, but finding it too deep for him he had to come out and go for further help. The workmen round about came up, and then Mr. Wild, • patient, came, and taking off his coat and waistcoat. jumned into the water and brought the deceaaed Ott. Wild, firet-clase patient in 11.0 estebl iehment, abniat ten minutes after eleven o'clock on Monday morning he heard that mmeone was in the pond, and going down he saw the deceased in the water, and he vent in and fetched her out. She was at the time about five yards from the ade of the pit, and apparently quite dead. Pr. Edward Lister, proprietor of the Havdock Lodge Retreat, roil on Monday, about eleven o'clock, one of the patients ran up to him crying that Mn, Vernon was in the pond, and he mn at once to the spot. When he got there : Mr. Wild yeas bringing the bode out of the water, and on exemir.ation he found the lady quite dead. Efforts were made and continued to restore animation for three quarters of en hour, but without mimes.. Deceased had a mark on her left eye, and another on the throat, evidently produced by etruggling. The fence amend the pond was about three feet high, and he had been satisfied with it up to the present dm, but • higher wooden one was to be erected for the future.
